documents.title: First Steps
documents.markdown:
Welcome! This page gets you from curious to contributing in about 30 minutes. Work through it top to bottom.

## 1. Get oriented (10 minutes)

* Read what [Next Society](https://next.ieb.net/society) is about: the overview of this collection explains the initiative, the Compendium, the missions and how content grows.
* Skim the [Compendium overview](/compendium/compendium). You do not need to read it all: pick the questions that catch your eye.
* Read the [Charter](/start/charter): our principles, roles and how decisions are made.

## 2. Join (10 minutes)

* **Request a wiki account** by writing a short note about yourself to team@next.ieb.net. You will receive an invitation by email. The wiki has no passwords: you log in with a link sent to your email address.
* **Complete your member page.** Every member gets a personal page under *Community → Members*. Add your interests and missions, what you or your organisation offer, and how people can best work with you.
* **Join the** [**chat**](https://next-society.zulipchat.com) and briefly introduce yourself: who you are and what drives you.

## 3. Find your place (5 minutes)

* Pick the mission closest to your interests and read its overview: [Next.Education](https://next.ieb.net/s/education), [Next.Economy](https://next.ieb.net/s/economy) or [Next.Democracy](https://next.ieb.net/s/democracy).
* Look through [Ways to contribute](/start/ways-to-contribute) for areas beyond writing: visuals, applications, outreach, partnerships.

## 4. Make your first contribution

Choose **one**:

* **Comment** on a page you read: a question, a source, a counter-argument. Select text and add a comment.
* **Take a task** without an owner from [Tasks](https://next.ieb.net/s/society/doc/tasks-liiESuzP6L): mention yourself with @ in the task line.
* **Plant a seed in the Jungle:** start a new page with an idea, an example from your practice or a first playbook recipe.

[Contributing](/start/contributing) explains how to do each of these in the wiki.

documents.title: Charter
documents.markdown:
*Version 0.3, November 2026. Proposed by the Leads. The Charter holds what we commit to; the* [*Handbook*](https://next.ieb.net/s/8a40c16b-eff6-4117-aac8-b31a2bfb2294/doc/handbook-XOaaldgP4w) *describes in detail how we work together. Comment on this page to suggest changes; see "Changing these rules" below.*

## 1. Principles

We want to work together on a shared understanding, not on detailed rules. Everything we do follows four principles:

* **Rough consensus and running code:** we prefer broad agreement and solutions that work in practice over long theoretical debates or full consensus.
* **Stewardship through contribution:** influence is earned through visible, high-quality contributions, not through titles or traditional hierarchies.
* **Subsidiarity:** decisions about content, partnerships and operations are made as locally as possible, by the people who are active in that area.
* **Transparency by default:** drafts, discussions and edit histories are open. We build in public to earn trust.

## 2. What we build

Next Society develops three things that build on each other:

* **Theory:** a foundation in science, humanistic philosophy and ethics. Part 1 of the [Compendium](https://next.ieb.net/s/compendium).
* **Missions:** outcome-oriented challenges that organise the transformation: Education, Economy, Democracy and Research.
* **Playbooks:** practical, open knowledge for acting on the missions. Peer-produced "recipes", for example: *How do I start a conversation about the transformation in the organisation I work for?* or *How do I find an organisation to work with if my current work feels stuck in today's economy?*

## 3. How content grows: Jungle, Garden, Park

To welcome new ideas without diluting the shared narrative, every page has a maturity:

| Stage | What it is | How a page gets there |
|:------|:-----------|:----------------------|
| **Jungle** | the wild, open space for new questions, ideas, experiments and early playbook recipes | Any member can plant a page. No approval needed; open for debate and editing by everyone. |
| **Garden** | tended content of a mission or area, actively reviewed, refined and connected to the bigger picture | When a Jungle page shows rough consensus (interest and practical value), a Lead of the mission or area adopts it. |
| **Park** | the curated core: the Compendium and matured playbooks. Our shared worldview, stable and citable | When the Leads of all affected missions and areas agree, or nobody objects within ten working days after it was announced in the Monthly Leads Meeting. The review checks rigour, coherence with the narrative and clarity. |

Each page shows its stage at the top: `Owner: @name · Status: Jungle | Garden | Park · Reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD`. All stages are public.

## 4. Roles

Everybody and every organisation can join. We work with five roles:

| Role | What you do | Where it shows in the wiki |
|:-----|:------------|:---------------------------|
| **Contributor** | Bring ideas, edits, sources, visuals or contacts. Comment, plant Jungle pages, take tasks. | Every member, credited on their member page and in the page history |
| **Co-Author** | Take responsibility for specific pages: review suggestions, keep them readable and up to date. | "Owner" in the page header |
| **Mission Lead** | Steward a mission: set its direction, organise its funding and partners, shape its narrative, invite and support contributors, distribute ownership, adopt pages into the Garden and decide together on the Park. | Listed on the mission's About page |
| **Area Lead** | The same for a cross-cutting area that serves all missions, such as Tech. | Listed on the area's overview page |
| **Partner** | An organisation that supports the initiative with reach, spaces or resources. | [Ways to contribute](/start/ways-to-contribute) |

Mission Leads and Area Leads together are the **Leads**.

**Rule of two:** every page and every mission or area has exactly two people responsible: Co-Authors for pages, Leads for missions and areas. Not one, not three: two give clear ownership and cover for each other.

**Succession:** if you want to hand over your role, help to find your successor. Until a mission or area has its second Lead, Max Senges serves as interim Lead.

**As we grow:** when missions get larger, Mission Leads can appoint **Co-Leads** for themes or working groups within their mission, and a small **Steering Group** can take over the decisions that concern NEXT as a whole. The [Handbook](https://next.ieb.net/s/8a40c16b-eff6-4117-aac8-b31a2bfb2294/doc/handbook-XOaaldgP4w) describes both roles and when we introduce them.

**Your profile:** your member page under *Community → Members* is your profile: interests and missions, what you or your organisation offer, how to work with you. Offers can be discussed openly, so reputation grows from real contributions.

## 5. How we decide

* **Locally first:** Co-Authors decide about their pages, Leads about their mission or area.
* **Monthly Leads Meeting:** all Leads meet once a month. They resolve questions across missions and areas, decide what moves into the Park, adjust how we work when practical friction demands it, and welcome new Leads. Rules are only added or changed when real problems require it.
* **Changing these rules:** changes to the Charter or the Handbook are proposed openly and open for comments for ten working days. The Monthly Leads Meeting then decides by consent: a change passes if nobody has a well-founded objection. If there is no consent within two meetings, a two-thirds majority of the Leads decides.

How we decide in detail, including everyday, urgent and important decisions and how objections work, is described in the [Handbook](https://next.ieb.net/s/8a40c16b-eff6-4117-aac8-b31a2bfb2294/doc/handbook-XOaaldgP4w).

documents.markdown:
How to work in this wiki in practice. For principles and roles, see the [Charter](/start/charter).

## Before you start

* **Small steps:** one idea or one improvement per change. Small changes are easy to review and to build on.
* **Ask the owner:** pages in the Garden and the Park have owners, shown at the top. For more than a quick fix, comment first or contact them.
* **Bigger topics:** start them as a new page in the Jungle and share the link in the chat.

## Comment

Select any text and add a comment, or use the comment field at the end of a page. Mention people with @ so they get notified. Comments are the main way to suggest changes to Garden and Park pages.

## Edit

* **Jungle pages:** edit freely. They are owned by everyone.
* **Garden and Park pages:** fix typos and broken links directly. For changes to content, comment first so the owner can include them.
* Every change is kept in the page history, so nothing gets lost.

## Create a page


1. Open the mission that fits your topic and create a new page there (or a sub-page of a related page).
2. Add the page header in the first line: `Owner: @you · Status: Jungle · Reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD`.
3. Keep it as an unpublished draft until it is ready to be seen. Published pages are public.

## Tasks

Any checklist item is a task. Write it as `task · @person · due YYYY-MM-DD` and it appears in the overview of all tasks and on the person's member page. Details at the bottom of [Tasks](https://next.ieb.net/s/society/doc/tasks-liiESuzP6L).

## Writing style

* **English**, clear and concise. Questions as page titles work well: they invite readers in.
* **Cite sources** in the text as (Author, Year) and add the full reference to the [References](/compendium/references).
* **Images:** only your own or openly licensed ones, with the source in the caption.

## How content grows

Pages mature from **Jungle** (open, anyone can plant and edit) to **Garden** (adopted and tended by the Leads of a mission or area) to **Park** (the curated core after review by the Leads concerned). The [Charter](/start/charter) explains the stages.

documents.title: Ways to contribute
documents.markdown:
Next Society is not a text to be consumed but a movement of practitioners who already work, lead and decide differently in their organisations and communities. There is more to do than writing. Find the area that fits you, then say hello in the [chat](https://next-society.zulipchat.com) or take a matching task from [Tasks](https://next.ieb.net/s/society/doc/tasks-liiESuzP6L).

## Missions and playbooks

Develop the content of a mission, share examples from your practice or write a playbook recipe. Start in the Jungle; the Mission Leads help it grow. → [Next.Education](https://next.ieb.net/s/education), [Next.Economy](https://next.ieb.net/s/economy), [Next.Democracy](https://next.ieb.net/s/democracy)

## Derivatives and applications

Turn the Compendium into slides, case studies, workshop formats, keynotes and briefings. CEOs, policymakers and civil society each need their own format. If you know one of these audiences, help translate the core ideas into their language.

## Illustration and visual language

The ideas need images that make them tangible and human, beyond generic tech aesthetics. Illustrators, designers and visual thinkers are invited to develop a visual world for Next Society. Start with [Brand & Design](https://next.ieb.net/s/8a40c16b-eff6-4117-aac8-b31a2bfb2294/doc/brand-design-dHpttFhrm6) and the open questions listed there.

## Open source AI toolkit

We use an AI toolkit with a brand book, assets and skills to create derivatives and illustrations. It currently needs paid accounts; we are building an open-source version for local use. Help with development and testing is welcome.

## Offers and co-delivery

Many of us advise, train or support organisations. Share your offers and reference projects on your member page and team up with others to support organisations in their transition, without giving up your own practice.

## Press and reach

Contribute media contacts, place guest articles, curate podcasts and bring our ideas into current debates.

## Collective action and politics

Open doors to associations, foundations, academies and politics: prepare hearings, co-sign statements and bring the missions to the places where the future is being decided.

## Partners

Organisations can support Next Society with reach, spaces or resources and become visible as partners. If you want to become a partner or recommend one, contact [Max Senges](https://next.ieb.net/doc/max-senges-dl7OqBs3E0).

# The Alchemy of the Next Societal Operating System

## *An Invitation to peer-produce a Blueprint for Human Flourishing in the Age of AI through Multistakeholder Missions & Playbooks in Education, Business & Democracy*

 ![](/assets/wiki/bafd74edcfcf4cb4.png)


# Abstract

The Next Societal Operating System is not shaped by technological determinism. It is a humanistic enterprise about the unfolding of human potential toward a desirable future. The recent and extrapolated advances in AI are expanding the feasible set of human action faster than our private, organizational and societal institutions can absorb. The risk is the Oblomov effect: the slow surrender of our human agency through convenience. This approach argues for a deliberate redesign of our societal operating system (SOS), proposed through three interlocking layers. Part One establishes the theoretical foundation: augmentation over automation, humans as agents not resources and a realistic-utopian north star for the transition. Part Two develops four Mazzucato-style societal missions that structure the path from today's socio-economic setup to the Next Education, Next Economy and Next Democratic Governance. Part Three offers transformation playbooks; namely concrete tools for individuals and organizations ready to lead rather than lag the shift.

***Keywords****: Next Economy, Societal Operating System, Augmentation, Oblomov Effect, Unfolding Human Potential, Capability Approach, Mission Economy, Transformation Stack, Oikonomia, Plurality, Realistic Utopianism, Entrepreneurial Mindset.*

## **Who started developing the Next Societal Operating System?**

*The Next Societal Operating System began as an open, self-organised collaboration among researchers and practitioners who share the conviction that AI's can be* *used to unfold human potential and should be deliberately turned toward promoting human flourishing. We* *also would rather help design that future than wait to see which one arrives. Contributors write in a personal capacity; the views expressed here do not necessarily reflect those of their institutions.*

**About this Compendium**

**Who funds the development of the Next Societal Operating System?**

*It is a self-motivated research-and-development venture, hosted by the Institute of Electronic Business at the University of the Arts Berlin. There is no external client and no commercial backer steering the work; most of it is done by contributors in their own time. We are open to collaborating with all stakeholders, and we would warmly welcome support — in kind or monetary — to deepen and broaden the effort.*

### How to read this Compendium

The narrative is organised around three Main Questions. Each question is answered through a series of smaller sub-questions, and every sub-question ends with 2–4 follow-up questions you can jump to next. Read linearly, read the questions that catch your eye, or treat the text as an adventure book.

### Why design a desirable future rather than critique the present?

This compendium is not a critique of what currently exists. There are enough of those. Instead, we are developing a north star for a desirable form of economy — one that aims at progressives AND conservatives. Our approach does not put forward demands. It is an enticing invitation. Every person, every organization can start tomorrow.

The critiques themselves — of digital capitalism (Zuboff, 2019), of platform extraction, and of the difficulties around maximizing monetary profits — are, in our view, largely established. We spend our effort instead on naming desirable directions concrete enough to build toward, because a society that can vividly picture a better future is far likelier to construct one (Polak, 1955).

### How did this worldview emerge, and how can you contribute?

The Next Economy is not authored from a single desk. It emerges as open knowledge, developed collaboratively in a Wikipedia-style process of peer production (Benkler, 2006; Weyl & Tang, 2023), with the explicit aim of composing a coherent worldview (Weltanschauung) for our conviviality and flourishing with AI rather than a loose anthology of opinions.

To keep that worldview coherent as many hands shape it, we use AI to help edit all materials — harmonising tonality, maintaining cross-references, and stress-testing the arguments and evidence. AI assists; it does not decide. The owner of each section remains accountable for its content, in keeping with the Human-in-Command principle this compendium argues for. Everyone is welcome to contribute: read our Collaboration and Governance Charter, create your contributor profile, and begin by commenting on the materials.

documents.title: Part 1: Leitmotif
documents.markdown:
Part One sets the theoretical and philosophical foundation of the socio-economic leitmotif. It opens with a diagnosis: AI is expanding what people can do faster than our institutions can absorb, and the central risk is not machine domination but the quiet surrender of agency through convenience, or what we call the Oblomov effect. From there it asks what an economy is actually for, why the present system does not self-correct and how technology should relate to human intelligence: as an amplifier of judgment rather than a substitute for it.

It then examines what AI cannot do — initiate, bear responsibility, begin something genuinely new — and the mindset we should therefore cultivate. Part One closes by arguing that the Next Societal Operating System is best understood not as a policy to be legislated but as a movement to be joined. The throughline is a conditional optimism: AI can widen human freedom and capability, but only if we deliberately re-design our institutions and govern its diffusion rather than letting the current dynamics play out.

**WHERE TO GO NEXT**

**→** [*Why should we worry about an "Oblomov Effect" in the age of AI?*](/compendium/why-should-we-worry-about-an-oblomov-effect-in-the-age-of-ai)

documents.title: Why should we worry about an "Oblomov Effect" in the age of AI?
documents.markdown:
![](/assets/wiki/d17e846566782d80.jpg)

There is a scene at the opening of Goncharov's *Oblomov* (1859) that should feel uncomfortably familiar in 2026. Ilya Ilyich Oblomov, a capable, educated Russian nobleman, lies on his sofa in his famous oriental dressing gown. Not because he is sick, not because he is wicked, not even because he is simply lazy. Being in bed has become, as the narrator puts it, his "normal condition." Every ordinary task — writing a letter to his landlord, attending to his estate, meeting old friends — presents itself as an insurmountable mountain. So he lies still, surrounded by gorgeous daydreams of a future he will never build. The novel ends with him fading away years later, his potential intact and unspent.

We use "Oblomovism"[^1] here as a shorthand for the slow surrender of agency in a person who has every objective reason to act. The strategic question for an AI-saturated society is whether something structurally analogous could unfold at socio-economic scale — and, more importantly, how we make sure it does not. Put positively: how do we make fulfilled, creative, entrepreneurial lives *more* likely because AI exists?

AI collapses the cost of producing competence-like output at remarkable speed. That is, in itself, extraordinary news: it lowers the threshold for entrepreneurship, learning and participation more than any technology since the printing press. But the first wave of empirical research also shows that convenience carries a cognitive and motivational price when delegation is unstructured, which is where the Oblomov metaphor stops being literary and starts being measurable[^2].

But research also shows that guided, reflective use of AI can *support* thinking, and that education and deliberate practice buffer the negative effects. That is exactly the point: the cognitive outcome of AI is a design variable, not a destiny. But the failure mode is now well described. It is a self-reinforcing loop — offloading reduces skill and confidence, which invites further offloading — operating simultaneously on individuals (the temptation of passive consumption of algorithmically curated comfort) and on institutions (the temptation to delegate judgment to systems that are faster but lack human perspective). Left ungoverned, this loop is the world's most efficient pipeline from freedom to paralysis: a high-tech Oblomovism in which agency is surrendered not under coercion, but through convenience.

### From warning to design brief

The answer this compendium proposes is therefore not a warning but a design brief. The two trajectories in front of us are both "man-made" and both genuine options. If we do not redesign the incentives and institutions that govern AI's diffusion, the technology will by default extend the extraction of attention, data and autonomy that the platform economy has already normalized. If we do redesign our Societal Operating System, the very same capability becomes a general-purpose augmentation layer: one that expands the feasible set of human action, restores time and attention for meaningful contribution, and distributes analytic and creative capability across a wider population than has ever held it. Self-efficacy, learning and plural participation then become the criteria against which deployments are measured — not residuals to be optimized away.

[^1]: A literary diagnosis, not a clinical one. [^2]: Three findings deserve attention. First, cognitive offloading erodes critical thinking when it becomes habitual. In a mixed-methods study of 666 participants, Gerlich (2025) found a significant negative correlation between frequent AI tool use and critical thinking ability, mediated by cognitive offloading — the tendency to delegate analysis, evaluation and memory to the tool. The effect was strongest among the youngest users; higher education acted as a protective buffer. Second, unreflective delegation impairs learning and deep processing. In an EEG study at the MIT Media Lab, Kosmyna et al. (2025) found that participants who wrote essays with LLM assistance showed markedly lower neural engagement, struggled to recall what they had just written, and underperformed when later asked to work without AI — a pattern the authors call "cognitive debt." Related work on knowledge workers (Lee et al., 2025) shows that confidence in AI shifts human effort from doing the thinking to merely checking its outputs. Third, the volitional system itself recalibrates. Across four experiments with more than 3,500 professionals, Liu, Wu and colleagues (2025) found that human–AI collaboration improved immediate task quality, yet when participants returned to unassisted work, intrinsic motivation dropped by an average of 11% and boredom rose by 20%. None of this proves an inevitable decline.

documents.title: How can a desirable future change an economy?
documents.markdown:
That redesign needs a north star. Fred Polak (1955) argued that civilizations rise or decline with the vividness of their images of a desirable future: a society that cannot picture a better world will not build one. Rawls (2001) added a guardrail, asking that such a vision stay "realistically utopian." Read this way, a North Star looks like motivation: a picture vivid enough to make people want to act.

That reading is true, but it does not go far enough. Imagining a desirable future also does economic work. The decisions that carry an economy, to invest, to hire, to found, and to lend, are made under radical uncertainty, where today's data cannot tell anyone how things will turn out. Beckert (2016) shows how actors close that gap with fictional expectations: shared images of a future state that make it reasonable to commit now. Investments flow toward believed futures[^3]. Getting our Next Societal Operating System believed in, then, is a contest of narrative as much as of evidence (Beckert 2016).

Futures studies has a name for this concept. In Inayatullah's Futures Triangle, three forces shape any decision: the weight of the past, the push of the present, and the pull of the future, the last of which he draws from Polak. What we are seeking is that pull. A desirable image does not pull because it is pleasant. If a promising future feels already underway or inevitable, it sedates, and the urgency to act today drains away. It only pulls when people believe they can shape it, when it is both desirable and *buildable*. This is the Oblomov effect read forward: comfort, and even optimism, will still end in inaction unless agency comes with them.

This vision is the north star we offer here. The Next Societal Operating System is more than a design brief: it is a candidate image of the future, our entry in that contest. It makes no claim to be the truest account. It earns its place by being realistically utopian, in Rawls's phrase: science-based enough to be buildable and desirable enough to be worth building. It only becomes real if enough of us deliberate on it on its own terms and come to desire its manifestation.

**WHERE TO GO NEXT**

**→** [*What is wrong with today's economy, and why isn't it self-correcting?*](/compendium/what-is-wrong-with-todays-economy-and-why-isnt-it-self-correcting)

**→** [*What can AI not do, and why does that matter?*](/compendium/what-can-ai-not-do-and-why-does-that-matter)

**→** [*What makes the Next Economy a movement rather than a policy?*](/compendium/what-makes-the-next-society-operating-system-a-movement-rather-than-research)

[^3]: Here we have to be honest, because the mechanism is indifferent to what it builds. The same expectation that funds a clean-energy build-out can inflate a bubble, and "AGI is around the corner, fund it now" moves real money whether or not it proves true. Fictional expectations explain why we act. They say nothing about which futures deserve it. Economics already knows the move: its models are an engine, not a camera, shaping the markets they claim to describe (MacKenzie 2006). Its measures do the same. GDP was never a neutral mirror; once it became the figure states and markets steer by, it made growth the measure of success (Coyle 2014). What this situation calls for is a different expectation for people to organize around, set on purpose rather than a tidier dashboard.

![](/assets/wiki/763a19c842d00613.png)

We are not in denial that modernity delivered real progress. Life expectancy has risen dramatically. Extreme poverty has plummeted. Literacy, access to medicine and personal security have improved across almost every region of the world (Pinker, 2018). These results matter and should not be dismissed.

And yet the current Societal Operating System (SOS) is exhibiting structural failure modes — a decoupling of capital and networked technology from the people and communities they are supposed to serve:

**1.** Capital has become globally mobile at super-human speed and complexity, while social and ecological costs remain local and lasting.

**2.** Networked tech and social media platforms optimize for operator value, not participant flourishing.

Being human has, as a result, been progressively reclassified: from a subject living a life, to a "human resource," to an attention unit and behavioral prediction input.

This is less a story of individual greed than of incentive structures — though the two clearly reinforce each other. It is a governance gap: extraction is measurable, financeable and scalable in ways that human flourishing is not (yet). The Next Economy must correct the categorical error at the heart of modern economics: treating the wellbeing of individuals, the household of families and of society, as well as the "household" of our planet as externalities.

If managing an economy well means managing society's household — *Oikonomia* vs. *Chrematistics*, the maximization of profit for its own sake — then waste, fragility, addiction and depletion are not side effects, but operating failures.

documents.title: What are economies actually for?
documents.markdown:
\
Every economic system embeds an implicit answer to the question: *what counts as doing well?* Mainstream economics answers with GDP growth, productivity and preference satisfaction. The Next Economy requires a different foundational metric: what people actually become and do.

The capability approach (Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2011) provides a basis for exactly this. "Development as freedom" — Sen's framework, which earned him the Nobel Prize — proposes that the expansion of substantive freedoms to live lives of value, not merely formal rights or average income levels, is the most adequate measure of progress. A society is doing well when its members can develop and exercise their central human capabilities: enjoy good health, use their senses and imagination, experience deep emotion, exercise practical reason, form social bonds, shape their political environment and live in relation to the natural world. ![](/assets/wiki/a1ebc8d5ae6e6642.png)

This framework grounds the humanistic AI vision (Senges et al., 2025): the purpose of artificial intelligence is not to maximize platform engagement or shareholder returns, but to allow every person to unfold their potential — which in turn allows for the enterprises they work at to unfold their potential. An AI system that automates drudgery and returns time and energy to allow for more collaboration, empathy, entrepreneurship and imagination.

documents.title: How should technology relate to human intelligence?
documents.markdown:
We are living through an epochal transition. The institutions of print society (nation-state, market, university, public sphere) have not disappeared, but they survive rather than strive in a world that organizes itself by a different logic: fluid, decentralized networks in which knowledge, capital and agency are constantly reconfigured (Baecker, 2007, 2018; Castells, 1996, 2009). Hartmut Rosa's diagnosis of social acceleration names the underlying mechanism: when technology, social change and the pace of life itself speed up faster than institutions can adapt, a widening gap opens between what is newly possible and what our institutions can absorb — and it is in that gap that agency is most easily surrendered (Rosa, 2005). ![](/assets/wiki/01a6e2fe353f4c7e.png)

A bet of the Next Economy is that this logic can be reconfigured. Open digital infrastructure enables a fundamentally different economy: decentralized social production in which commons can emerge that are economically non-rivalrous and socially transformative (Benkler, 2006). Doug Engelbart (1962) already articulated the right vision sixty years ago: technology as an *intelligence amplifier*, not a substitute for human judgment. The chess world named this pairing “centaur” — humans provide judgement and steering, while the AI provides its  calculating capability — that same division of labour is what augmentation now extends to knowledge work, where human-in-command judgement paired with machine capability outperforms either on its own. Weyl and Tang (2023) extend this into governance: digital technology, properly designed, can vastly extend our capacity to collaborate across differences, with diverse communities retaining their distinctiveness while cooperating through interoperability rather than homogenization. ![](/assets/wiki/82e9ccc6e04c1b24.jpg)

documents.title: What can AI not do, and why does that matter?
documents.markdown:
![](/assets/wiki/f5e707c1a883609e.png)AI demonstrates competence without comprehension. AI systems defeat grandmasters, synthesize diagnoses and generate fluent prose without ever understanding what victory, disease, or argument means in human terms (Dennett, 2017). They operate efficiently and at scale, but without teleology or intentionality. Human understanding is, moreover, embodied: meaning, salience and perspective grow out of being a living body in a world rather than out of disembodied symbol-processing — part of why these systems' fluency is not the same as comprehension.

A clarifying distinction comes from Arendt's (1958) analysis of human activity. She distinguishes *Labor* (producing and distributing food and basic-need articles), *Work* (engineering and fabricating artifacts of the durable artificial world) and *Action* (the irreducibly political domain of collective world-building and shared commitment). AI can progressively take over Labor and increasingly support Work. What it cannot do is Action in Arendt's sense, or what she called "genuine initiation of new enterprises" or *natality* — the capacity to start something that has never existed before. Between Work and Action sits the step the convenience trap most easily captures: the move from thinking to deciding. Oblomov is not paralysed for want of thought but for want of resolution — and it is judgment, the willingness to choose, commit and bear the consequences, that carries a person from weighing options to initiating something genuinely new. ![](/assets/wiki/8743b9749975f867.png)

Intelligence itself is better understood as an ecosystemic principle running through all living systems, not an exclusively human attribute (Bridle, 2022; Agüera y Arcas, 2025). In this meta-perspective, the human role is not to compete on output volume but to retain stewardship of teleology — the capacity to ask: *why, toward what? What should grow? What do we want to become?*

This has direct practical consequences for the Next Economy. The more AI takes over Labor and Work, the more time and energy is freed for Action. This is the empowering face of automation. The dangerous face is the Oblomov effect: if relief from drudgery flows into passive consumption rather than creative action, natality is squandered. Every hour that AI frees, the question *"what will you begin?"* returns[^4].

Freed time converts into creative Action only when people are secure enough to use it that way — precarity tends to fill the gap with worry rather than initiative — and AI can add cognitive load even as it removes manual load, since reviewing and steering machine output is its own kind of effort (Kosmyna et al., 2025).

documents.title: What mindset do humans need to thrive alongside AI?
documents.markdown:
AI now puts a tireless "thinking partner" and knowledgeable personal tutor within reach of almost anyone, lowering the cost of learning, building and starting things further than any tool since the printing press. Using it well, though, asks something of us, beginning with how we understand "AI" itself. The first element of a thriving mindset is epistemic. "AI" reaches most people not as a neutral fact but as a discourse, painting a powerful, ideologically charged narrative. Both the AI salvation story and the human extinction story are strategic projections while we venture into an indeterminate future[^5]. The appropriate starting posture is therefore neither dread nor awe, but calm critical distance: AI systems are human artifacts, their surrounding narratives are made by people, and we are free to examine the premises rather than inherit them. Maintaining that distance requires basic literacy about how the technology works, a degree of social-critical awareness about who benefits from which narrative, and the habit of consulting plural sources.

What moves people to get up from the sofa? Decades of empirical research give a clear answer. Sustained intrinsic motivation requires three conditions: *autonomy* (action genuinely flows from one's own will), *competence* (the experience of being able to act effectively) and *relatedness* (embeddedness in meaningful relationships) (Deci & Ryan, 2000). Complementing these, contemporary positive psychology finds that human flourishing has five measurable dimensions: positive emotions, deep engagement in meaningful activity, high-quality relationships, a sense of meaning and belonging to something larger than oneself, and accomplishment (Seligman, 2011). These are not abstractions. They are the architecture of an entrepreneurial life design (Gedeon, 2024).

Enter *self-efficacy* — the belief in one's capacity to produce an effect in the world — as the source of volition. It is not a fixed trait. It is a nurtured and trained capacity, built through mastery experiences, role models, social endorsement and solved challenges (Bandura, 1997). It is the psychological foundation of entrepreneurship: the willingness to initiate, to take ownership, to co-create solutions rather than wait for instructions. *Given that in a fully AI-enabled economy each worker will have to assess the opportunities they could work on and opt for the one that offers the most promising value production, this mindset is not optional but essential for all workers.* Educational and organizational architecture in the Next Economy is therefore fundamentally an architecture of entrepreneurial mindset and practice. Two honest qualifications belong here. This is an invitation, not a norm: a flourishing society should widen people's options — including the option of quieter, less entrepreneurial lives — rather than press everyone into the same posture. And people do not begin from equal psychological, social, economic or health positions, so a humanistic societal architecture worth the name should build pathways inside existing institutions and active support for those who do not already arrive self-directed, instead of quietly selecting for the already-confident. ![](/assets/wiki/6238acd11e8accda.png)

Using AI in the zone of proximal development. Training self-efficacy points directly to how AI should be used. Vygotsky (1978) showed that humans develop most powerfully in the zone of proximal development: the band of challenges just beyond what one can master alone, but reachable with the support of a more capable partner. AI is the first technology in history that can play this scaffolding role on demand, for anyone, in almost any domain. Used this way, it is a magnificent engine of curiosity: an instant supplier of knowledge, a patient explainer, a generator of communities around special interests. The same tool, however, can also be used one notch lower, below one's own competence, as a substitute rather than a scaffold, and this is where the convenience trap of the opening paragraphs sit. A thriving mindset, therefore, includes a deliberate relationship to friction: knowing what convenience does to skill and will, and consciously preserving hurdles, solving problems oneself first, drafting before prompting, verifying rather than accepting. Learning science calls these "desirable difficulties" (Bjork, 1994): the effort is not an inefficiency to be optimized away; it is where the growth happens, and where our humanity is exercised. Working well with AI is therefore not only a matter of friction but of disposition: it rewards reflective, critical-thinking people who can be specific, ask precise questions and communicate in situation-realistic terms rather than defer to fluent output.

Even more important than the *how* (entrepreneurship) is the *why*. The deepest motivational lever — what carries people through crisis — is not happiness or comfort but the experience that one's action is part of a larger context (Frankl, 1959). Crucially, this Why does not have to be discovered in isolation. It can be provided by an organization, a movement, or a shared vision of a desirable future — which is precisely what a compelling north star for the Next Economy aims to offer. The individual who joins a mission-driven enterprise, a regenerative community, or a peer-learning network finds their personal Why amplified by a collective one. People who hold a vivid image of a better future they can help build are systematically more motivated, more resilient and more creative than those who do not. This is the spirit of Ivan Illich's conviviality: the tools worth having are simple, accessible, transparent and adaptable enough that people can shape them rather than be shaped by them[^6] (Illich, 1973).

In network-society terms, the progression from *socialized mind* to *self-authoring mind* to *self-transforming mind* (Kegan, 1994) is not a personal luxury but strategic societal infrastructure[^7]. A self-authoring person has an internal value system and the metacognitive capacity to consciously choose which networks to participate in and which to resist, and, increasingly, which tools to merely use and which to truly own. This is also the mindset of the entrepreneur and intrapreneur. The Next Economy needs this capacity mainstreamed as a cultural baseline, not as an elite trait, because in a fully AI-enabled economy, every employee and citizen benefits from embracing self-leadership, collaborative ownership and active participation in shaping the systems they inhabit.

The mindset, compressed: no fear, but no naivety either. Curiosity at the edge of one's competence. Deliberate friction where convenience would erode skill and will. And ownership of one's attention, one's tools and one's future. Use the technology to shape the world, not to be passively shaped by it.

 ![diagram](/assets/wiki/a2dfbffc8cccf713.jpg)             *Illustration 1 - Kagan’s Constructive Development Theory (Ken Norton - Brigthedonats)*

**→** [*Mission 1 — How do we make human-potential development the primary "business" of society?*](/compendium/mission-1-how-do-we-make-human-potential-development-the-primary-business-of-society)

**→** [*Where do I start in the first 90 days? (The Entry Protocol)*](https://next.ieb.net/s/compendium/doc/where-do-i-start-in-the-first-90-days-the-entry-protocol-qeQiCvHgbh)

[^5]: Often projections of their authors' own psychological constitution, resting on premises that cannot currently be proven (for instance, that intelligence is inherently competitive, or that capability implies a will to dominate). Recognizing this matters not only intellectually but psychologically: fear is not a neutral state. It narrows attention, crowds out reflection and suppresses precisely the critical faculties a citizen of the AI age needs most. [^6]: Agency toward AI is not only a matter of inner posture; it has a material dimension. As long as the capability lives exclusively in a few centralized platforms, users remain recipients of prefabricated, pre-digested experiences designed around someone else's incentives. The countermove is appropriation: experimenting with local and open models, building one's own workflows, frameworks and agents, personalizing the technology around one's own questions and projects. This is both an individual practice and a structural preference: a Next Societal Operating System should favor decentralized, interoperable, locally controllable AI over monolithic dependency, because the distribution of technological ownership is the distribution of agency. [^7]: A socialized self whose identity is anchored in external roles and expectations is systematically vulnerable to algorithmic manipulation and to Oblomovism. The vulnerability, though, runs wider than any single anchor: anyone who has not practised critical questioning is exposed, whatever their identity rests on.

documents.title: What makes the Next Society Operating System a movement rather than research?
documents.markdown:
The Next Societal Operating System and its missions are not only a policy agenda or a business model, it is a transnational movement that integrates solidarity and sufficiency by growing a coalition of individuals, enterprises, communities and institutions that cross-promote and support each other's transformation, thereby generating synergies and momentum that no single actor could create alone. ![](/assets/wiki/f151ad8863f93d4b.png)

Two wisdom traditions inspire the anthropological foundation. [*Ubuntu*](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubuntu_philosophy&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1782050018697007&usg=AOvVaw0OeMeVTp3lRpmSD4Gs0Fgd) (South African for "I am because we are") anchors individual identity in community: not the isolation of the autonomous individual, but resonance with others is the place where human potentials genuinely unfold. And [*Tikkun Olam*](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikkun_olam&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1782050018697408&usg=AOvVaw2eZ0IzCSHaNUiFVA6-vxkO), the Hebrew concept of repairing the world, asserts that every person bears co-responsibility for the whole: the small actions of everyday life, heal or break the world. Together they frame the deeper Why of the movement. Bell Hooks (2001) adds a third strand to this relational anthropology: the good life is interdependent. The capable person, in her account, is compassionate and strong, autonomous and well-connected, taking responsibility for self, intimates and society at once and understanding these responsibilities as finally inseparable (Hooks, 2004).

There is a hard strategic and economic logic here that complements the ethical one. Movements generate network effects. Organizations that participate in and actively support the Next Societal Operating Eco-System gain access to a trust network and talent pipeline that isolated actors cannot replicate. This is the coopetition logic of the Next Economy: competing on differentiated value while cooperating on shared infrastructure, norms and narrative. Peer-production — genuinely collaborative value creation in which participants are not bound by hierarchy — has already demonstrated through open-source software, Wikipedia and Creative Commons that it can generate resources of extraordinary quality and scale (Weyl & Tang, 2023). The same logic applies to the economic and civic ecosystem of the Next Societal Operating System. ![](/assets/wiki/17aabc540cebfde6.jpg)

In the age of algorithmized connection, the quality of human community has become the decisive differentiating dimension. The deep experience that one's presence and contribution are genuinely desired — also known as *Belonging* — is not a soft nicety. It is a productive force. Organizations that design work as community and meaning-space generate stronger commitment, lower attrition and higher innovation. Movements that successfully weave belonging across organizational boundaries create the critical mass needed to tip systems toward new equilibria. The Next Societal Operating System is built one enterprise, one community, one deliberate beginning at a time, but those beginnings compound when they recognize each other as parts of the same direction of travel. Belonging at this scale is not automatic; it rests on communication literacy and the courage of simplicity — the everyday craft of making oneself understood and of understanding others — which AI can support but cannot supply for us (Schulz von Thun, 2021). Nor is sheer scale the whole mechanism: movements of this kind spread less like a simple virus than through complex contagion, in which people take up contested new practices only after repeated, reinforcing contact with several others who already have (Centola, 2018), so durable change rests on a web of relationships and communities of practice rather than on headcount alone (Wenger, 1998; Wheatley & Frieze, 2006).

documents.title: Part 2: Missions
documents.markdown:
*The Missions*

Part One argued *why* a Next Societal Operating System is desirable and *what* normative ground it stands on. Part Two turns to the harder question of *how* a society might coordinate itself to get there. The main organising logic we adopt is Mariana Mazzucato's mission economy (Mazzucato, 2021): rather than leaving transformation to the aggregation of market signals or reducing it to top-down industrial policy, a mission framework sets concrete, time-bound, outcome-oriented goals that are ambitious enough to require cross-sectoral mobilization among public institutions, private enterprises, research communities and civil society all pulling in the same direction. The Apollo "Moonshot" program is the canonical reference; more recent analogues include the EU's Horizon missions or the city of Amsterdam's mission to become a circular economy. Missions are neither forecasts nor subsidies; they are *shared public problems expressed as design briefs*, around which markets, research agendas and regulatory instruments reorganize themselves. For the Next Societal Operating System we propose four such missions: **(1) make human-potential development the primary "business" of society; (2) redesign economic architecture beyond GDP; (3) upgrade democracy and governance for the third millennium; (4) ensure research co-evolves with AI.** Each is a grand challenge in its own right; taken together they describe the socio-economic setup a humanistic AI age requires. ![](/assets/wiki/65082b9e9cfe6bc3.png)

The current document concentrates the depth of its treatment on Missions 1 and 2, with Missions 3 and 4 outlined as companion trajectories that can be developed in subsequent work. The asymmetry is deliberate. Mission 1, addressing human-potential development, or *Bildung* in the Humboldtian sense, is *the transformation engine* of the whole system. It provides the fertile ground on which flourishing becomes possible and the precondition for the other missions to succeed. Without a population equipped with agentive literacy, self-efficacy and entrepreneurial imagination, redesigned metrics remain abstractions, democratic upgrades misfire and AI-accelerated research outruns the human judgment that is supposed to steer it. Mission 2, deals with establishing the economics of the desirable future(s), is the second focal point because it is where the Next Economy actually "lives". If we cannot specify what we are optimizing for *instead of* GDP, and how value creation, investment, pricing and accounting are supposed to recognize stewardship of human and planetary flourishing, the Next Economy remains a slogan rather than a system. Missions 3 and 4 are no less important, as they shape the institutional scaffolding (democracy, governance, knowledge production) that keeps Missions 1 and 2 honest over time, but they are treated here as sketches, inviting the community to co-develop them.

documents.title: What design principles hold the Next Societal Operating System together?
documents.markdown:
The shift to the Next Economy is best understood as a portfolio shift: away from optimizing for profit extraction, toward optimizing for human flourishing. Four design principles hold the system together.

**Education as primary transformation engine.** Not a sector among others, but the decentralized agency-training ground that defines system capabilities like peer-production competence and entrepreneurial agency. Investment in human capability is the highest-return investment a society can make.

**Decentralized but interoperable.** Local autonomy generates resilience; open standards enable collaboration and scalability without monopolized choke points. The internet itself is proof of concept (Open Knowledge Foundation, 2025). Plurality extends this principle from technology to governance and culture (Weyl & Tang, 2023).

**Commons + shared assets + private expression.** Some goods function best as commons or public-private partnerships (education, health, core digital infrastructure). Some assets can be shared to reduce waste (tools, vehicles). Private property remains essential where it expresses identity, culture and individual creativity.

**Governance that is machine-readable but human-legitimate.** Rules should be machine-readable and executed consistently, while decision accountability remains human. Auditability, legibility, contestability and participation are non-negotiable conditions for democratic legitimacy in an AI-enabled governance system.

**Regenerative and relational by design.** A Next Societal Operating System does not merely avoid harm; it actively restores the social and ecological foundations it depends on, staying within Raworth's (2017) social and planetary boundaries rather than breaching them. It also treats the quality of relationships — with oneself, with others, and with future generations — as core infrastructure rather than a by-product. Long-term, intergenerational stewardship (Krznaric, 2020) is therefore a design constraint, not an afterthought: institutions are judged in part by whether they widen or narrow the options available to those who come after us.

These principles provide the ground for four grand challenges in the spirit of mission-economy thinking (Mazzucato, 2021).

documents.title: Mission 1 — How do we make human-potential development the primary "business" of society?
documents.markdown:
In a fully AI-enabled economy, the central productive work is no longer generating outputs. It is producing capable, self-directing humans. That sounds obvious, but most education systems still behave like credential factories designed for an industrial labor market.

The Next Economy (and Next Societal Operating System) requires a different key performance indicator: *Human Agency Capacity per capita*. This means designing learning environments and services that build self-efficacy, self-directed learning capacity and entrepreneurial competence as default mindsets and behaviors. The capability approach (Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2011) and the humanistic AI framework (Senges et al., 2025) provide the normative ground: *Bildung* (education as the lifelong cultivation of the whole person) is the institution most directly responsible for expanding what people can be and do.

### Why is education the keystone mission of the AI age? And how do we make agency Europe's decisive capability in the AI age?

Europe's AI debate is almost entirely about supply. Compute, capital, frontier labs, industrial policy. All of it is necessary, none of it is sufficient. A continent can buy every GPU on the market and still lose, if it has too few people and institutions able to act while AI accelerates everything around them: too few who can initiate, judge, build, govern. That capacity is the scarce input of the AI age. Education is where it is formed or lost. This is why Mission 1 comes first.

The point is not to turn education into an instrument of geopolitical competition. It is to recognize that a society's sovereignty ultimately rests on the agency of its people and institutions. Without that agency, infrastructure remains inert, regulation becomes theatrical, and values lose their carrier.

In every other domain this approach touches, the choice between augmentation and automation is a question of outputs. When AI substitutes for human work in a factory or a law firm, we lose jobs or quality, and we can argue about the trade. In education the same choice operates one level deeper. It decides whether the capacity to act comes into existence at all. ![](/assets/wiki/9a211262b4e32b4a.png)

Self-efficacy is built through mastery experiences: challenges actually faced, problems actually solved, projects actually finished (Bandura, 1997). The danger is not that AI makes learners lazy. It is quieter and more serious than that. A badly designed AI learning environment removes the productive struggle through which self-efficacy, initiative and judgement form. It removes it invisibly, while the learner stays formally on track and feels productive. Essays drafted, problems solved, projects planned by the machine before any competence has formed. The result is a graduate with credentials and without the capacity to begin.

**So one rule should govern every design decision in this mission: AI must become a scaffold for agency, not a substitute for the experiences through which agency is formed.**

The same failure mode scales. [Europe2031](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://europe2031.ai/&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1782050018709350&usg=AOvVaw18Y9oCObz81a8rTBQElky5) names it at the level of a continent: a society can keep every procedure intact, its elections, its courts, its universities, and still lose the ability to shape its own future. Oblomovism works the same way in a person and in a whole society. Both start to fall apart in the same place: where the ability to act was meant to grow and quietly never did.

This is why Mission 1 is the transformation engine of the Next Societal Operating System. Redesigned metrics (Mission 2) stay inert numbers unless people can act on them. Upgraded democratic instruments (Mission 3) misfire without citizens who can weigh evidence and change their minds in public. AI-accelerated research (Mission 4) outruns human judgment unless that judgment was formed somewhere first. Every other mission in this approach presupposes what only this Mission produces.

Meanwhile, the institution responsible is losing its traditional product. When AI can pass the exams that certify human competence, certification and capability come apart. The exam may still test something worth knowing. But it can no longer certify independent human capability unless the assessment also verifies process, judgment, transfer and agency. Most educational institutions still run like credential factories built for an industrial labor market, optimizing for the one output AI has just made cheap: reproducible performance.

### What is the Next Education Mission?

AI saturation is a matter of years, not decades, so our Mission runs on two horizons: a strategic-readiness horizon for the institutions deciding now, and a generational horizon for the people still being formed.

**By 2031, Europe has made Human Agency Capacity a strategic capability.** Every school, university, public administration and major workforce-development system uses AI to expand human initiative rather than replace it. Every public AI deployment in education and training passes an agency audit. And Europe publishes agency-capacity indicators alongside literacy, numeracy and AI capability.

**By 2035, every young person leaves formal education having initiated and completed at least one real project with impact beyond the classroom.**

Waypoints inside that window:

**›** **By 2027:** agency-audit prototypes piloted in schools, universities and public-sector AI-training programs.

**›** **By 2028:** hands-on frontier-AI capability becomes a professional requirement for senior public-sector decision-makers: regulators, judges, procurement leads, university leadership and other public leaders whose decisions shape AI deployment.

**›** **By 2029:** public procurement of AI learning and training tools requires both a human-agency audit and a strategic-dependency audit.

### What do we mean by Human Agency Capacity?

The **psychological layer** is the disposition to act: self-efficacy, autonomy, competence and relatedness (Deci & Ryan, 2000), and a growth orientation toward one's own capability. Validated instruments for all of these already exist (Bandura, 1997).

The **behavioral layer** is action itself: initiating, persisting, completing, reflecting, collaborating, and transferring what was learned into a context it was never taught in. This layer exposes whether the disposition is real. ![](/assets/wiki/86b50e0b08de75c6.png)

The **outcome layer** is the trace agency leaves in the world: real projects completed, ventures founded, civic contributions made, self-directed learning pursued, professional transitions navigated, community initiatives started.

Read together, the three layers start being something a system can pilot, track and improve. The instruments are not the problem; assembling them and committing to count them is. The OECD's Learning Compass already names student agency and co-agency as the goals of education for 2030 (OECD, 2019).

Counted, the index belongs on Mission 2's beyond-GDP dashboard, next to health, ecological and wellbeing indicators (Stiglitz, Sen & Fitoussi, 2009; Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2011). Human Agency Capacity per capita is the form of societal wealth that education produces, and the first new measure the dashboard can pilot at meaningful scale, because the instruments are validated and the institutions to run them already exist.

### How do we keep AI from hollowing out the learning it touches?

One instrument carries this mission, let's call it the **agency audit**. For every AI system deployed in a learning or working context, measure what it does to the human using it.

The **human agency delta** comes first. After a semester with the tool, do learners initiate more or less? Persist longer or quit earlier? Can they now do without it what they could not do before, or can they no longer do without it? The same technology produces both outcomes. An AI tutor built as a coach inside a real project builds capability. The identical model built as an answer machine removes the productive struggle that capability grows from. The audit separates augmentation from automation at the exact point where the difference matters most.

Europe2031 adds a second measurement, and it is the one that turns this mission into sovereignty policy. The **strategic agency delta** asks whether the deployment increases Europe's own institutional competence, autonomy and leverage, or deepens dependency on external platforms, models, data infrastructures and closed systems.

That dependency can be audited. Does the institution understand the system well enough to govern it? Can it change providers without losing its data, workflows and accumulated competence? Are standards open, interfaces portable, and outputs contestable? Does learning accumulate inside the institution, or only inside the vendor relationship? Does the procurement contract create exit options, or lock-in? Does the deployment build local expertise, or outsource judgement behind a user interface?

Both deltas run across the whole surface: AI tutors, school platforms, university tools, public-sector training systems, workforce-development programs. The agency audit is the concrete, measurable form of the question this approach keeps asking: is AI expanding human capability, and for whom? With one clause added: expanding Europe's, or someone else's?

### What existing models show the mission is feasible?

No country runs this at national scale yet. That is the reason it is a mission: missions name what does not yet exist and commit to building it. But working models exist at every level of selectivity, which disposes of the standard objection before it lands: that agency-based education only works for the already-agentic.

**›** **School 42** runs tuition-free, peer-to-peer software schools in many countries, with no teachers, no lectures and no fixed curriculum, only peer review and real deliverables.

**›** **Alemannenschule Wutöschingen**, a German School Prize winner, is a public school in a small town that selects no one at the gate: no fixed classes, no grades, no textbooks, students running their own learning journeys with learning companions.

**›** **Minerva University and Olin College** prove the model at the selective, demanding end, with active-learning seminars, real projects early, and transferable thinking valued over content delivery.

**›** **CODE University of Applied Sciences**: a state-accredited German university built around project-based learning, self-directed inquiry and venture creation.

The pattern across all four is a single move. Learning is treated as production, not consumption. Real projects, fast feedback, peer learning, public consequences, steadily increasing autonomy. None of these is conclusive national evidence. Each is proof that the model survives contact with reality, at a village school and a selective college alike.

The objection deserves a direct answer anyway. Kegan's research suggests most adults never reach the self-authoring stage under present conditions (Kegan, 1994). Read one way, that number says the mission is hopeless. Read correctly, it says the mission is large. Kegan's stages describe what environments produce, not what people are born with; mastery experiences, role models and social endorsement are design variables (Bandura, 1997). The binding constraint is rarely the students alone; it is the learning architecture around them. Alemannenschule matters because it takes every child in its catchment area. ![](/assets/wiki/c60745323c4000a0.png)

And the economics just moved in the mission's favor. Bloom (1984) showed that one-to-one tutoring beats classroom instruction by two standard deviations, a result no school budget could ever afford to scale. AI makes mastery learning affordable for the first time in history. Whether it arrives as a coach or an answer machine is not fixed by the technology. It is a design decision societies make.

### Whose agency are we building, and for what kind of Europe?

The blunt form of the institutional argument: a Europe whose regulators, judges, civil servants, university leaders and procurement officers cannot competently use frontier AI will not govern frontier AI well. You cannot regulate, adjudicate or buy what you have never operated. Retraining programs file this under skills gap. It is an agency gap, and it is urgent in a way the generational horizon is not, because these are the people deciding now. Closing it is [*Bildung*](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bildung&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1782050018717719&usg=AOvVaw26CuTp5uZU9de4BuZjIR8l) across the lifespan, not a certificate course. One implication runs straight into Mission 3: deliberative democracy presupposes citizens who can read a balanced brief critically and change their minds in public. That is a learnable capability, which makes it a curriculum question.

And not only Europe. While grounding our anthropology in Ubuntu we cannot stop our mission at Europe's borders. Europe is the first place we implement this mission, not its boundary. While states compete for energy and minerals, the input that actually compounds is human capability, and Europe's answer to the AI age cannot be a fortress. It has to be a coalition: co-built capability institutions, local ownership, shared leverage, with middle powers and across the Euro-African relationship in particular.

The test for any such partnership is the one this compendium applies throughout. Does it expand capabilities on both sides, or does it extract human potential into someone else's AI stack? That is the strategic agency delta again, now at the scale of continents. Ubuntu gives the only durable answer: I am because we are. A capability built so that one side owns and the other depends is not a partnership.

documents.title: Mission 2 — How do we redesign economic architecture beyond GDP?
documents.markdown:
GDP is a useful accounting tool but an increasingly weak strategic compass in a world where many digital goods approach zero marginal cost, where global capital markets operate at unfathomable magnitudes and speeds and where the main risks are systemic. The Next Economy needs an evolved operational framework — one that is both philosophically grounded and practically compelling to business leaders.

*Oikonomia*, what the Greeks considered the art of good stewardship of the household, is not nostalgia. It is a framing for our missing control system. Aristotle's distinction between *Oikonomia* and *Chrematistics* (wealth accumulation as an end in itself) identifies precisely the categorical error of contemporary economics. Three converging frameworks make this operational: ![](/assets/wiki/3aa4be84fb316847.png)

**›** The **Doughnut model** (Raworth, 2017) defines the safe and just space between nurturing the social foundation and not breaching the ecological ceiling.

**›** The **Common Good Economy** (Felber, 2010) translates this into corporate governance: capital is a tool, not the goal.

**›** **Commons peer-production and governance** (Ostrom, 1990; Benkler, 2006) demonstrates that shared resources can be created and managed sustainably across centuries without either privatization or state control. For the cases that fall between market and commons, market design offers a complementary tool: Alvin Roth's Nobel-recognised work on matching markets (Roth, 2015) shows that well-specified domains — kidney exchange is the canonical example — can be allocated fairly and at scale without using price as the deciding signal. Its power is real but bounded: it works where the problem can be precisely defined, not as a general substitute for deliberation about ends.

Two movements show how this philosophy is already being adopted in business practice without sacrificing commercial ambition. Conscious Capitalism (Mackey & Sisodia, 2013) argues that business is inherently good and that its highest expression rests on four tenets: a higher purpose beyond profit, stakeholder integration, conscious leadership and a conscious culture. Companies like Patagonia, Costco, Southwest Airlines and the Container Store, operating on these principles, have consistently outperformed their sectors financially while building the trust and loyalty that competitive moats based on opacity cannot replicate. Beautiful Business (Morris, 2022; Leberecht, 2015) frames every enterprise as a "fundamental creative journey" whose power rests on integrity, curiosity, elegance, love as connective tissue and magnetic differentiation. These are not soft values; they are precisely the capabilities that AI cannot commoditize.

### Where will value shift in the AI economy?

 ![](/assets/wiki/b0763a37c673dba2.png)

Organizing markets around human life areas — rather than legacy industries — clarifies where the Next Economy's wealth creation will concentrate. Building on Jacobides, Cennamo & Gawer's (2018) theory of ecosystems as a distinct governance form held together by modularity and non-generic complementarities, the Ecosystemizer framework (Kawohl & Krechting, 2022) maps ten life areas, and Table 1 below assesses their relative trajectories in an AI-saturated economy: In plain terms, an ecosystem here is a set of interdependent products and services that create value together and that no single firm fully owns or controls — which is why it is more illuminating to map human life areas than legacy industries.

| Ecosystem Domain | Relevance/Jobs in the Next Economy | Business-Model Shift |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------|:---------------------|
| Health & Wellbeing | Up (aging + prevention + AI triage) | Treatment transactions to prevention platforms + human care delivery |
| Unfolding Potential (Education) | Up sharply                         | New credentials to capability products: mastery evidence, apprenticeships, communities |
| Personal Security (digital + societal) | Up sharply                         | Point solutions to continuous assurance, identity, auditability |
| Entertainment    | Up sharply                         | Content (AI/video/games) to live shows and real-world experiences |
| Personal Mobility | Mixed: efficiency up, labor down   | Ownership to shared fleets, orchestration, routing |
| Industry         | Output up, labor down              | Linear production to flexible, localized, circular systems |
| Living           | Mixed                              | Architecture, real estate, furniture, home improvement |
| Consumption      | Mixed                              | Food, fashion, personal tech — quality > quantity shift |
| Relationships & Community | Up                                 | Matching & facilitation to membership, belonging, verified safety |
| Belief / Mindfulness / Meaning | Up                                 | Content to practice communities, rituals, guided development |
| Sustainability (cross-cutting) | Up (hard constraint)               | Green tech and ESG reporting to measurable circularity and regenerative operations |

Table 1 — Next Economy Scenario Forecast

The pattern across all domains: value migrates from output volume (cheapened by AI) toward trust, care, creative orchestration, imagination and experience. All of these aspects require irreducibly human capabilities — the qualities that both Conscious Capitalism and Beautiful Business have long argued are also the sources of durable competitive advantage.

For incumbent companies, the transition has a four-step logic:

**1.** Identify the strengths and weaknesses of your current business model given the Next Economy outlook. (Where do you profit from lock-in, opacity, or externalized costs?)

**2.** Define your 2050 North Star and adapt or re-invent your business grounded in stewardship for the Next Economy.

**3.** Move from products to ecosystems. Orchestrate interoperability and partner capacity rather than hoarding it.

**4.** Energize and train your stakeholders to embrace the transformation journey.

**WHERE TO GO NEXT**

**→** [*Which transition archetype fits my organisation?*](https://next.ieb.net/s/compendium/doc/which-transition-archetype-fits-my-organisation-In9QshIJbm) *(Part Three) — if you want the incumbent-by-incumbent path through the value shift.*

**→** [*Mission 3 — How do we upgrade democracy and governance for the third millennium?*](/compendium/mission-3-how-do-we-upgrade-democracy-and-governance-for-the-third-millennium) *(Part Two) — the governance layer that has to keep pace with the economic one.*

### What is the Changing Role of Money in the Next Economy?

For centuries, money has served as humanity's most effective coordinating mechanism. By acting as a unit of account, a medium of exchange, and a store of value, financial capital built the industrial world, lifted billions out of poverty, and drove unprecedented technological innovation. In today's economy, maximizing financial return is the logical North Star for any enterprise.

However, the defining characteristic of a free market is its ability to adapt to shifting realities. The Next Economy is not a rejection of market dynamics; rather, it is the market's rational response to the profound shift in scarcity brought about by Artificial Intelligence.

**From the Scorecard of Success to the Infrastructure of Flourishing.** As AI and automation drive the marginal cost of intelligence, analysis, and routine production toward zero, we are entering an era of unprecedented abundance in areas that used to be highly constrained. When standard cognitive labor becomes commoditized, money loses its monopoly as the ultimate differentiator of value. ![](/assets/wiki/c7b1163d8e7b2e78.png)

In the Next Economy, the role of money matures. It transitions from being the *ultimate metric of success* (the ceiling) to the *essential infrastructure of stability* (the ground).

We recognize that money remains strictly necessary. It is the fuel that keeps the economic engine running. However, just as a logistics company does not exist simply to hoard fuel, a Next Economy enterprise does not exist solely to hoard capital. Money is recognized as a vital means to a higher end: the unfolding of human potential and the stewardship of complex, resilient ecosystems.

**The Market Dynamics of the Transition.** *Why would profit-driven incumbents voluntarily change the role of money in their organizations?* The answer is not moral obligation; it is competitive advantage. The transition to the Next Economy is already being driven by collective interest and positive market dynamics over time.

**1.** **The Talent Market Premium:** As AI democratizes basic capabilities, the true bottleneck for enterprise success shifts to uniquely human traits: trust, natality (the ability to initiate the genuinely new), complex orchestration, and deep empathy. The individuals who possess these highest-leverage capabilities will not trade their finite time purely for maximized financial compensation, especially once their baseline stability is secure. They will gravitate toward organizations that offer the richest environments for capability expansion and flourishing. Enterprises that continue to treat money as the sole lever of motivation will suffer a severe brain drain, losing top talent to Next Economy competitors.

**2.** **The Innovation Imperative:** When companies focus solely on financial extraction, they optimize for the known, stifling the psychological safety required for breakthrough innovation. By treating capital as an investment in human flourishing rather than a dividend to be extracted, Next Economy enterprises create the conditions for long-term, non-linear innovation. They out-compete legacy firms not by squeezing margins, but by inventing entirely new markets.

**3.** **Ecosystem Resilience as Risk Mitigation:** Smart capital abhors systemic risk. The rigid maximization of short-term profit often externalizes costs onto society and the environment, creating fragile supply chains and volatile markets. Investors and market leaders are increasingly recognizing that aligning capital with collective human and ecological interests is the most rational form of long-term risk management.

**The Pragmatic Path Forward.** For incumbents and conservative leaders, the transition to the Next Economy does not require abandoning fiduciary duty. It requires elevating it.

Capitalism is evolving. The organizations that will dominate the next century are those that understand that money is no longer the product of the machine. The true output, the ultimate source of value creation and competitive moats in the AI age, is a flourishing, deeply capable and highly trusted human workforce. By realigning financial capital to serve human capital, leaders can harness the positive market dynamics of the Next Economy, ensuring their organizations remain not only profitable, but deeply relevant.

**WHERE TO GO NEXT**
