documents.title: Mission 3 — How do we upgrade Democracy and Governance for the third millennium?
documents.markdown:
Public-sector capacity — especially the capacity to co-create and co-lead public-private partnerships as missions — becomes a strategic priority in a fully AI-enabled economy. It becomes the difference between shared prosperity and failed states. When Rules as Code and Rulemapping make bureaucracy faster and decisions fairer, government functions like permitting, compliance, benefits administration, procurement, justice and participation become more important, not less.

### Upgrading democratic participation

Several instruments have proven themselves as means to improve decision quality and citizen engagement:

**›** **Liquid Democracy** — vote delegation to trusted persons on specific issues — can increase informed decision density and participation simultaneously. The German Pirate Party's implementation of Liquid Feedback from 2010 onward, Taiwan's vTaiwan digital consultation process (which successfully co-created Uber and platform economy regulation with 200,000+ participants) and multiple academic analyses of liquid delegation mechanisms demonstrate that the approach increases policy information content and citizen engagement when properly implemented (Blum & Zuber, 2016; Ford, 2002).

**›** **Quadratic Voting** (Lalley & Weyl, 2018) reduces extremist majority decisions by assigning progressive costs to multiple votes, giving minority preferences appropriate weight.

**›** **Deliberative Democracy** — randomly selected, informed citizens who assemble to share their views — has demonstrated in more than a dozen countries that informed civic self-determination produces wiser decisions than parliamentary horse-trading. Stanford's Deliberative Democracy Lab, led by James Fishkin and Alice Siu, has conducted over 150 Deliberative Polling experiments in more than 50 countries, consistently finding significant depolarization and more nuanced policy preferences after deliberation. In the landmark "America in One Room" experiments, satisfaction with democracy among Republican participants doubled from 24% to 50% after a weekend of structured deliberation (Fishkin et al., 2021). A 2024 follow-up confirmed that these attitude changes have lasting effects beyond the deliberation event itself (Fishkin et al., 2024). ![](/assets/wiki/f2c77683a400e37c.png)

A critical enabler of all these participatory approaches is the quality and balance of the information participants receive. Fishkin's method relies centrally on carefully balanced briefing materials — documents that present the strongest arguments for and against each policy option, reviewed by all parties for accuracy and fairness before distribution. Wikipedia's Neutral Point of View (NPOV) policy offers a scalable model for agreeing on factual "ground truths" that can serve as a baseline in propaganda-prone online discourse. Evolving and institutionalizing NPOV-style briefing norms across media and civic spaces is one of the most powerful structural instruments available for reducing the influence of algorithmic polarization and disinformation on collective decision-making. It is worth stating the ambition plainly: the goal is not merely to consult citizens but to move from participation toward genuinely collaborative, co-creative decision-making, in which those affected help shape the options rather than only react to them.

Plurality (Weyl & Tang, 2023) extends this further: digital technology, properly designed, can give genuine voice to diversity rather than flattening it into majoritarian compromise or winner-takes-all scenarios. The architectural ingredients are: diverse communities, interoperating through open standards, collaborating on shared challenges without surrendering local distinctiveness. This is the political analogue of the decentralized-but-interoperable paradigm discussed for technology architecture.

### Rules as Code: making justice executable

Rules as Code is a progressive innovation project at the OECD and many countries that aims to create machine-readable codifications of laws, policies and administrative procedures in order to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of bureaucracy. Early implementations in Germany, France, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Australia and Singapore demonstrate automated compliance checking, transparent decision systems and substantial efficiency gains. Equitable tax distribution, near-real-time social support decisions and mechanisms like Tobin taxes on financial transactions to fund global common goods become practically achievable through this infrastructure (OECD, 2020). In Germany, the Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND) has invested into "Rulemapping" to turn tangled regulation into navigable, machine-readable structure. ![](/assets/wiki/96fe9d1eee186059.png)

This mission's legal and governance requirements are non-negotiable: *auditability* and human accountability for each rule application; *legibility* (citizens must be able to understand why a decision happened); *contestability* (an affordable path to challenge outcomes); and *participation* in rule creation and governance at scale. These must trump other mission objectives.

**WHERE TO GO NEXT**

documents.title: Mission 4 — How should research co-evolve with AI?
documents.markdown:
If transformative AI has fully enabled the Next Economy, research becomes both the biggest lever and the largest risk surface. As discussed, the economics agenda will have extended beyond growth; we will have a research agenda with decisive themes like wealth distribution, power concentration, information integrity, safety and the transition dynamics that can trigger social crises.

### Dual financing architecture

For large-scale, long-horizon problems — climate adaptation, public health preparedness, resilient infrastructure, education system redesign — that require patient capital and coordination, mission-driven public-private partnership investments make most sense. This is not state versus market; it is a public-private portfolio (Mazzucato, 2013).

Open science and shared research infrastructure becomes the default choice when AI systems become a core research substrate, as access to compute, data and evaluation tooling determines who can produce insights. A public and interoperable AI research infrastructure — offering compute credits, shared benchmarks, open repositories and replicability requirements — is essential for research on questions of political and systemic interest. The principle Romer (1990) established holds: knowledge is non-rivalrous; the more it is shared, the more value it creates.

### How researchers work with AI

AI accelerates literature mapping, hypothesis generation, simulation and parts of experimentation. But this increases rather than decreases the premium on epistemic discipline: reproducibility, ensuring dataset integrity and governance of model behavior. Research in the Next Societal Operating System is less like solitary genius work and more like human–AI co-production inside well-governed collaborative pipelines, consistent with the peer-production logic of Plurality.

The human researcher's irreplaceable role is teleological and contextual: *What is the right question? Which values guide the search? What are the implications of a finding for actual people and communities?* That is the organ of natality that AI cannot substitute. It is also embodied and situated: a researcher feels the stakes for particular people and places in a way a model does not, which is one more reason the choice of question cannot be wholly delegated.

**WHERE TO GO NEXT**

**→** [*What can AI not do, and why does that matter?*](/compendium/what-can-ai-not-do-and-why-does-that-matter) *(Part One) — the teleological role of the human researcher is a specific case of the irreducible human capacities named there.*

**→** [*Why is human flourishing a competitive advantage, not a charitable add-on?*](https://next.ieb.net/s/compendium/doc/why-is-human-flourishing-a-competitive-advantage-not-a-charitable-add-on-xtZZGwJuZw) *(Part Three) — epistemic discipline and judgment are exactly the capabilities AI will not commoditize at scale.*

**Mission 1:** *How do we make human-potential development the primary "business" of society?*

This page is the entry point to Next.Education. The full mission is described in the Compendium: [read Mission 1](/compendium/mission-1-how-do-we-make-human-potential-development-the-primary-business-of-society).

## Mission Leads

Two Mission Leads look after this mission together (Rule of Two, see the [Charter](/start/charter)). To be named.

## Current focus

What the mission works on right now. To be defined by the Mission Leads.

## How this space is organised

* **Tasks:** open tasks of the mission.
* **Meetings:** minutes and decisions of our joint work.
* **Jungle:** ideas, drafts and open questions. Everyone can add a page.
* **Playbooks:** practical guides from our practice, growing from Jungle to Garden.
* **Outputs:** finished work such as slides, briefings, workshop formats and events.

## Get involved

New here? Start with [First Steps](/start/first-steps), comment on any page, take an open task or say hello in the [chat](https://next-society.zulipchat.com).

Practical guides for organisations and communities, built from the practice of our members. Each playbook is a sub-page, titled as a question, with concrete steps and examples from practice.

* New playbooks start with **Status: Jungle** and are open for everyone to improve.
* The Mission Leads promote a playbook to **Garden** once it is tested and consistent.
* Matured playbooks are listed in [Compendium Part 3](/compendium/part-3-playbooks).
